description: Our team aims to encourage children to enjoy and learn through interactive game about space and Earth.
summary:
Our group developed an interactive game for 7-12 year old learners. This game encourages young learners to build interest in and deepen their knowledge of human survival on the Moon and Mars. 


This addresses the challenge by making the game setting unique, where players aim to invade Earth as Martians. In addition, we decided to set the game on Mars, which allowed our group to focus on providing information specifically about Mars acquired through NASA's open data source. 


This project is essential for sharing collected information among generations. Since, even though there are many facts and data discovered by NASA and associated organizations, it is barely recognized among the population who are not familiar with NASA open data sets.
details:
LAST HUMAN ON MARS is an interactive game where the player is the only human alive on Mars, ruled by AI. The player will collect resources to survive on Mars while escaping from the AI pursuers. The player's ultimate goal is to gather sufficient resources to launch a rocket to return to their hometown, Earth.

How does it work?

First, the player chooses either keyboard or motion-tracking technology to begin the game. The motion-tracking technology detects the player's facial, shoulder, and arm movements and converts them into the character's movements.

Figure 1: Selecting Game controls

After learning the game's setting and ultimate objective, players are guided through a tutorial. The basic motions in the game are often made intuitive, such as walking, turning, and grabbing resources. However, the tutorial is necessary for players to recognize what is critical for survival and how to avoid those situations, including radiation and solar storms.

Figure 2: Tutorial Screen

As players complete the tutorial, they are free to move around and collect resources to launch the rocket. However, players should be mindful of damage accumulated by being exposed to radiation and solar storms, which are explained in the tutorial.

This game incorporates the resources from NASA open data sets within the visual information as well as the explanations given when the player is exposed to radiation, solar storms, and resources on Mars, such as sulfur crystals. Moreover, there is some trivia that is randomly displayed in the upper left corner of the screen, including the necessary amount of oxygen and food per day for one astronaut.

As the player escapes from Mars, the game reveals whether they have successfully returned to Earth. To survive the 180-day journey back, the player must have collected sufficient oxygen and food resources on Mars. The players will also be ranked based on their survivability and the amount of resources they collected on Mars.

How are NASA’s open data sets utilized?

1. Solar Storms

This feature uses four coronal mass ejections (CMEs), phenomena in which gas is ejected from the Sun, recorded by NASA between May 10 and 14, 2024. Based on the time of occurrence and speed, the game determines the order, intervals, and intensity of the storms. When a storm approaches in the game, the date and speed of real solar storms in the past are displayed on the screen.

2. Oxygen and Food

According to NASA standards, each astronaut consumes 895 g of oxygen and 800 g of food per day. Since the game uses these figures, collecting 1.6 kg of food, for example, will provide 2 days’ worth for the journey to Earth.

3. 180 days to go back to Earth

Based on the return journey to Earth outlined in NASA's crewed Mars exploration plan, if you gather enough supplies to last 180 days, you'll be able to board the return rocket.

4. Limit for radiation

The game uses the 600 mSv limit, which is set by NASA as the maximum lifetime radiation exposure for astronauts, as the threshold for failure.

5. The Ground setting

The ground on which the player walks is based on 37 photographs of Gale Crater taken by the Mars rover's “HiRISE” camera.

6. Resources to collect

The four types are sulfur crystals, mudstone containing organic molecules, soil containing water, and rock samples collected by the drill. All of these were actually discovered or collected by the Mars rover “Curiosity,” and the rankings reflect the amount of each sample brought back.

7. Additional Information about Mars

The page also provides information on the radiation level observed on Mars (0.67 mSv per day), the length of a Martian day (24 hours and 39 minutes), and the intensity of sunlight (about 43% of that on Earth). These three pieces of information are displayed on the screen for reference in the upper left corner.

Benefits

The game is designed for students aged 7–12, including those who are and who are not interested in space.

  • The survival game helps players to understand the essential resources required for human survival under extreme conditions.
  • Players can learn about extreme conditions and available resources on Mars through activities and brief explanations displayed on the screen.

Intended impact

  • The game introduces the environment on Mars through an immersive geological representation
  • The game indirectly teaches players about the consequences of their decisions by presenting them with choices, such as whether to collect essential resources while enduring radiation exposure or avoid AI pursuers by hiding, and allowing them to experience the outcomes of their actions.
  • It keeps players entertained with interactive motion capture and the excitement of survival and escape, as well as competitiveness stimulated by global ranking displayed after the player escapes from Mars.

Figure 3: Motion-capture technology incorporated in the game

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We used SI (AI) as a development assistant, not as the source of the idea. The concept — the last human escaping an AI-controlled Mars city, played with your body through a webcam, collecting real Mars discoveries — and every design decision were made by a human team member.

SI tools: Claude Code (Anthropic Claude models) wrote most of the game code and automated tests under human direction, summarized official rules and NASA data sources, drafted on-screen English text, and cross-checked every NASA number against its source. OpenAI Codex reviewed the code for bugs.

In the game itself, Google MediaPipe Pose (an on-device machine-learning model) reads the player's body from the webcam; no camera data leaves the browser.

No SI(AI)-generated images, video, or voice are used. Mars ground imagery is real NASA/JPL/University of Arizona (HiRISE) data.

How is your project creative?

Motion-capture technology

We incorporated motion-capture technology that detects players' movement and reflects it in the game. We consider it creative because motion capture allows players to move their bodies freely while enabling them to interact with the game environment in an intuitive and immersive way.

Survival and escape game feature

Our group thinks the survival and escape features of the game are creative because they encourage players to make strategic decisions under pressure while facing the difficulties of surviving in an unfamiliar and extreme environment on Mars.

What factors did your team consider?

We focused on creating an escape game to help players learn about Mars’ environment and resources. In the game, players take on the role of the only human living on Mars. With the planet completely under the control of AI, their goal is to gather the resources needed to launch a rocket and escape. By making it essential not only to collect resources but also to secure the oxygen and food necessary for human survival and to avoid radiation, the game allows players to experience firsthand the harsh realities of life on Mars.
